# Prompting FLUX

Models: FLUX.3. A good prompt runs about 900 characters.

Name each reference where the prompt uses it as `@{ref:<ref>}`, with the exact ref you pass; Sceneform swaps in the model's own token, so wherever this guide names a token (`@Image1`, `Figure 1`), write the mention instead.

FLUX reads a plain description of the finished image. There is no special syntax, and every phrase should name something you could point to in the frame.

**Order.** FLUX pays the most attention to what comes first, so lead with what matters most. Black Forest Labs' default order: one opening sentence for the image type and medium, then the subject and what it is doing, then the setting, then the light, then framing and lens. "High-angle black and white photograph with a grainy film texture" sets the look before any subject appears. When framing matters, put the subject and its framing before the environment: "a person with a determined expression, forest fire in the background, close-up" rather than "a person standing inside a forest fire, close-up".

**Length.** FLUX.3 expands a short prompt into a detailed caption on its own, so add sentences only for what must be controlled: positions, appearance, light, text. On FLUX.2, 30 to 80 words suits most images. FLUX.2 Klein does no expansion: what you write is exactly what it receives, so write it out in full prose.

**Sentences for relationships.** Use sentences for who holds what, what stands behind what, and where the light falls. Short phrases are fine for style, palette and effects.

**Photographs.** Name the camera, lens or film stock instead of writing "professional photo", then say what that look does to the picture: "shot on Kodak Portra 400, natural grain", "35mm lens at f/1.4", "early digital camera, flash photography, slight noise". Describe light by its source, direction and quality, and say what it touches: "soft window light from the left", "harsh direct flash that casts sharp shadows against the wall". For realism, describe what a real camera records, such as visible grain or slight chromatic aberration at the edges; "highly detailed" and "ultrarealistic" add nothing. One or two effects at most.

**Colour.** A hex code works when it is tied to one named object and introduced with the word "color" or "hex": "the car is in color #FF5733". A loose "use #FF0000 somewhere" is unreliable.

**Text in the image.** Quote the exact words with the capitals and punctuation you want, say where they sit, and describe the type by weight, case, colour and character: "a paper poster on the wall that reads "OPEN LATE" in bold red condensed sans-serif". Mention text early, give each block its own position in reading order, and keep strings short: long strings render less accurately. Among the FLUX.2 models, Flex is the one tuned for typography and small detail.

**Edits.** Write the change as an instruction in three parts. Name the target precisely enough that only one thing matches, by position, size, colour, or what it sits next to. Say what it becomes. Then name what stays: "Replace the cherries in the right-most jar with multi-colored sprinkles. Change nothing else." For several changes at once, give each its location, then a preserve list that names the scene's major elements one by one rather than "the rest of the image". For a person, name the preserved details: "keep her pose", "preserve her identity, head position, and lighting". Prefer a specific verb, "change the clothes", over "transform the person".

**Several attachments.** Refer to each by the same words every time and give each one a role and a relation to the others: the person from the first image wears the jacket from the second and stands in the kitchen from the third. Say how the pieces fit, including where the light comes from: "put the bottle on the counter, label facing the camera, lit by the window on the left".

**Avoid.** Negative phrasing: the prompt has no negative syntax, and Black Forest Labs' fix for an unwanted element is to describe what fills that space instead: "an empty promenade" for no crowds, "a plain studio backdrop in one colour" for no clutter, "clean, unmarked surfaces" for no text. In an edit, removal is an instruction and works: "Remove the cat from the sofa." Quality tags such as "masterpiece". Vague style labels such as "aesthetic" or "vintage" where a concrete medium, era or film stock says more.
